memories.memory: I earn about $78,000 a year as a public-sector program coordinator, and I automatically move $450 from each paycheck into a separate savings account.
In February 2025, I put $6,500 of my savings into a small equipment-rental business run by a former coworker, even though the investment agreement says I could lose the entire amount.
I still owe roughly $9,200 on my truck loan, with monthly payments of $386 scheduled to continue until November 2028.
When my father needed urgent home repairs last summer, I paid the contractor $3,100 and arranged for him to repay me in installments rather than taking out a loan.
I have about $31,000 in my workplace retirement plan, but I reduced my contributions for six months to cover a professional certification and moving costs.
A payroll error in October 2024 deposited an extra $1,240 into my account, and I had to return it through three deductions from later paychecks.
I keep around $2,000 in cash at home for emergencies because my work sometimes requires short-notice travel to remote communities where card payments are unreliable.
